items.title: Joint Region Marianas and University of Guam Launch Campaign to Defend Native Wildlife
items.author: Joint Region Marianas Public Affairs Office
items.summary: ASAN, Guam (Sept. 17, 2026) - Joint Region Marianas and the University of Guam have partnered to launch the "Båsta BTS" campaign, a community-driven initiative aimed at controlling the invasive brown treesnake, or Boiga irregularis, and preventing its spread.
items.body:
ASAN, Guam (Sept. 17, 2026) - Joint Region Marianas and the University of Guam have partnered to launch the"Båsta BTS"campaign\, a community-driven initiative aimed at controlling the invasive brown treesnake\, or Boiga irregularis , and preventing its spread.

Båsta means, “to put a stop to,” in CHamoru. The goal of the campaign is to stop or prevent the expansion of BTS to neighboring islands.

With the tag line, “Learn. Spot. Protect Native Species of the Marianas,” the campaign utilizes agency partnerships, educational materials, and hands-on workshops, to empower the military community to identify, report, and prevent the spread of invasive species such as the BTS.

The campaign has already produced two successful BTS Control Workshops with nearly 200 participants of all ages.

“Preventing the dispersal of the BTS via military transport remains a paramount priority for JRM," said Leanne Obra, JRM natural resource specialist. "Through these workshops, we are empowering residents to actively manage and protect our natural resources. It is vital that we halt the spread of invasive species, because if the BTS were to reach neighboring Pacific islands, it would pose a catastrophic threat to both their environment and their economy.”

Each year, the federal government invests more than $7 million in two vital areas: BTS interdiction to prevent the accidental transport of snakes off Guam, and environmental conservation to control the local snake population and restore native habitats. Educating military families on these biosecurity measures is key to keeping nearby islands like Saipan, Tinian, and Rota safe, protecting these sensitive areas and securing the training grounds essential to regional defense.

To get everyone involved, the "Båsta BTS" campaign hosts interactive, family-friendly BTS Control Workshops and Snake Hunts annually. Participants learn about different snake control tools, how to identify BTS in a forest canopy at night, and how to safely handle, capture, and humanely dispatch a snake.

"The loss of our native wildlife to the brown treesnake creates a ripple effect that destabilizes Guam’s entire ecosystem,"explained Tayah Hawley, UOG extension associate."Outreach is our bridge to the public. When we actively engage the community and promote awareness, we build the essential local support required to protect our endangered species and combat this invasive predator."

Annual Workshops are made possible through collaboration with multiple agencies and organizations, each providing unique demonstrations, expertise, and educational activities. Contributing agencies include the Colorado State University Center for Environmental Management of Military Lands, University of Guam, U.S. Department of Agriculture-Wildlife Services, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Guam Department of Agriculture – Division of Aquatic & Wildlife Resources, U.S. Geological Survey Fort Collins Science Center, USGS Pacific Island Ecosystems Research Center, and the National Parks Service.

The most recent snake hunt was conducted Aug. 28 at Asan Beach Park and the next BTS Control Workshop and snake hunt is scheduled for October 17.

For more information or to get involved with the "Båsta BTS" campaign, please email btsoutreach.cesu@gmail.com.

items.body:
SCOTT AIR FORCE BASE, Ill. — More than 30 Army Reserve Soldiers of the Aurora, Colorado-based 7450th Medical Operational Readiness Unit, a downtrace unit of the Army Reserve Medical Command hierarchy, trained and operated as the patient insertion team in synchronization with other military and civilian personnel during Exercise Ultimate Caduceus 2026, henceforth known as UC26, here Sept. 7-12, 2026.

UC26 is a U.S. Transportation Command-led annual patient movement field training exercise held here, Alpena, Michigan; Boise, Idaho and Fort Campbell, Kentucky. Approximately 400 military and civilian personnel from AR-MEDCOM downtrace units, USTRANSCOM, U.S. Northern Command, U.S. Strategic Command, U.S. Air Force aeromedical evacuation crews, Critical Care Air Transport Teams, U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, Defense Health Agency, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and myriad commercial partners all coordinated with each other in the shared responsibility in ensuring unity of effort.

In addition to the 7450th MORU Soldiers, more than 40 personnel from the 7451st MORU out of Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Washington comprised of the exercise control element, known in military parlance as the “white cell,” and live role-players to supplement the manikins prepared as simulated patients.

U.S. Army Reserve Maj. Jesse Back, commander of Headquarters and Headquarters Company, 7450th MORU and the officer in charge of the PIT crew, said the FTX replicates large-scale patient reception at point of injury, immediate first aid and triage, patient movement and transportation, in-flight care and continued care in medical treatments inside and outside of the continental United States.

“The mission of the PIT is to provide manpower to help execute the large-scale patient movement exercise that Ultimate Caduceus is, and so we are the manpower to help move patients through the tracking process to help them understand the mission,” said Back.

Part of the duties and responsibilities of the PIT crew were to prepare the simulated patients by using manikins with various injuries and effects, applying moulage and prosthetics to both the simulated patients and live role-players.

Additionally, the PIT crew facilitated and executed the ground aspect of patient movement and distribution — loading and off-loading patients, respectively to and from tactical airlift, rotary-wing and light transport aircraft such as the C130J Super Hercules, U.S. Army UH- 60L Black Hawk and C-12 Huron; as well as multiple commercial aviation and Civil Reserve Air Fleet platforms.

Back also said the PIT crew not only was a vital component in the joint-service, interagency network of patient movement, care and transportation — it is wholly conducive to readiness assessment and validation for his crew and the rest of the exercise participants.

“Our mission helps with the understanding of large-scale combat operations because as we are moving the patients through, they’re getting validated by each section the CCATT; the doctors and the nurses all through the patient process line,” Back said. “We’re the ones intricately moving those patients through those steps, so that way they can get good, solid training and to help them have a successful exercise.”

U.S. Army Reserve 1st Lt. Suenomi Cobb, a medical-surgical nurse assigned to the 7450th MORU, said her training experience as a member of the PIT crew enriched her understanding and appreciation of interoperability with U.S. Air Force personnel.

“It was awesome to see the Air Force and how they operate on the aircraft and how they communicate,” Cobb said. “From what I learned here, I’ll be able to take back the Air Force’s way of loading and off-loading patients, how we communicate with one another, especially with the loud engines running in the aircraft.”

Moreover, the Grand Rapids, Michigan denizen said she was able to perform in other roles in UC26 outside of the PIT crew.

“I actually got the opportunity to be a simulated patient for the Air Force,” said Cobb. “They loaded me onto a C130(J), I flew all the way to Idaho and en route I was a behavioral health patient, so I got to simulate a mental health crisis onboard the aircraft.”

Overall, UC26 and other joint-service, interagency field training exercises ensure that the Army Reserve medical enterprise is sufficiently trained and equipped for mobilization in tandem with interoperability partners in support of large-scale combat operations and large-scale mobilization operations.

“We’re getting good teamwork training, we’re communicating, we’re getting back to the basics as far as litter carries which some people haven’t had since Basic Training and just overall, patient movement,” said Back.

“Just understanding how we interact with our partners, because this is a global exercise — multiple Air Force partners, Navy and other (DoW) partners to help understand where we fit in that mission set.”

items.body: On Sept. 16, under the direction of U.S. Southern Command, Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere (JTF-WHEM) forces successfully interdicted a floating refueling station supporting illicit at-sea drug trafficking operations in the Eastern Pacific. Intelligence confirmed the vessel's involvement with the Los Choneros violent narco-terrorist organization. Individuals removed from the vessel have been transferred to Ecuadorian authorities. After clearing the vessel and disembarking the crew, U.S. forces sank it. JTF-WHEM continues to conduct precise and professional operations to dismantle the logistical networks fueling narco-trafficking in the Western Hemisphere. "Alongside our Ecuadorian partners, we are relentlessly pursuing narco-terrorists who prey on our citizens, undermine hemispheric security, and leave death and suffering in their wake. This deliberate, lawful, and precise operation saves lives and makes our citizens—from Ecuador to the United States—safer," said the commander of U.S. Southern Command, Marine Gen. Francis L. Donovan.

items.title: NORAD F-16s Deploy to High North Under Operation ARCTIC VANGUARD
items.author: Alaskan Command Public Affairs
items.summary: The Alaskan NORAD Region (ANR) deployed Eielson Air Force Base F-16 Fighting Falcons to Goose Bay, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada, in support of Operation ARCTIC VANGUARD (OAV) 26-4.2, from Sept. 13–26, 2026. During this North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) operation, ANR is operating directly alongside the Canadian NORAD Region (CANR) to execute critical defense missions across the Arctic.
items.body:
JOINT BASE ELMENDORF-RICHARDSON, Alaska – The Alaskan NORAD Region (ANR) deployed Eielson Air Force Base F-16 Fighting Falcons to Goose Bay, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada, in support of Operation ARCTIC VANGUARD (OAV) 26-4.2, from Sept. 13-26, 2026. During this North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) operation, ANR is operating directly alongside the Canadian NORAD Region (CANR) to execute critical defense missions across the Arctic.

Under OAV 4.2, NORAD personnel and aircraft will forward deploy into Greenland to execute operations in austere conditions alongside partners from both the Kingdom of Denmark and NATO. This operation supports the NORAD and U.S. Northern Command Nordic Bridge concept, which aligns the commands’ Arctic operations, exercises and training, activities, and investments with other U.S. Combatant Commands, NATO, individual nations, and regional partners.

The deployment of Eielson’s F-16s, supported by Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF) strategic airlift, demonstrates agile combat employment across vast geographic seams, validating NORAD’s capability to rapidly maneuver multi-role combat airpower from the Pacific theater into forward Arctic operating locations. By staging combat aircraft through northeastern Canada and forward into Greenland, the operation confirms that combined forces can disperse, sustain, and generate air superiority missions in extreme sub-zero, infrastructure-austere environments while validating integrated aerospace warning and control interoperability across regional command boundaries.

“Operation ARCTIC VANGUARD demonstrates that austere conditions and vast distances present no barrier to NORAD’s collective defense,” said Lt. Gen. Robert D. Davis, Commander, Alaskan NORAD Region. “Deploying combat airpower from Alaska across Canada and forward into Greenland validates our agile combat capabilities and demonstrates our seamless integration with the Canadian NORAD Region, the Kingdom of Denmark, and our NATO allies. Together, we maintain continuous vigilance and credible deterrence across North America’s northern approaches.”

Operation ARCTIC VANGUARD is part of a recurring series of NORAD and U.S. Northern Command operations conducted across the North American Arctic to enhance presence, operate from forward Arctic locations, and defend North America’s northern approaches.

Under the Nordic Bridge concept and efforts to bring orchestration to Arctic operations, activities and investments, OAV enables more consistent presence of multinational forces in the region, operating in multiple domains, in varying locations.

items.title: AI military targeting may move faster than humans can authenticate, critics warn
items.author: Natalie Oliverio
items.summary: AI military targeting may move faster than humans can authenticate, critics warned during a Wednesday hearing in Washington.
items.body:
A U.S. Navy guided-missile destroyer fires a Tomahawk missile in support of Operation Epic Fury, Feb. 28, 2026. (U.S. Navy)

Human approval may not be enough to ensure manual control over AI-enabled decisions , witnesses told Congress Wednesday, as artificial intelligence takes on a greater role in military target identification and recommendations, and in turn, compresses time available to intervene.

The concern, critics say, is not limited to weapons that can select and engage targets on their own.

At the hearing, titled “Artificial Intelligence in the Military Domain: Implications for Human Rights,” witnesses told members of the Tom Lantos Human Rights Commission that AI can influence human decisions leading to a strike while leaving the individual formally responsible for the final call.

“The approval button alone does not demonstrate the control,” Anna Mysyshyn, a Ukrainian AI-governance researcher, told lawmakers.

The issue comes as the Pentagon pushes to use AI to accelerate military decision-making. The Pentagon’s 2023 AI adoption strategy identified “fast, precise and resilient kill chains” as a desired outcome, while its 2026 AI strategy calls for becoming an “AI-first” warfighting force by redesigning military workflows and operational concepts around current AI capabilities.

Mysyshyn questioned whether a person supervising multiple AI-enabled systems can recognize an incorrect recommendation and intervene fast enough before harm occurs. She cited Ukraine as an example of AI compressing decisions from hours to minutes.

In many scenarios, a human making the final decision does not necessarily have enough information, time or the ability to challenge the system’s recommendation, she said.

The Defense Department’s 2023 directive on autonomy in weapon systems requires autonomous and semi-autonomous weapons to allow commanders and operators to exercise appropriate levels of human judgment over the use of force.

Wednesday’s testimony focused on a broader question: whether that judgment remains meaningful if AI is influencing targeting faster than a human can authenticate.

Amanda Klasing, national director of government relations and advocacy at Amnesty International USA, warned that AI can compress the military “kill chain” in ways that make it difficult to determine whether meaningful human discernment actually occurred before a strike.

Joseph Chapa, a former military officer and scholar of military ethics, argued that the debate should not focus solely on how autonomous a system is. He urged policymakers to consider whether an AI system relies on statistical inference, what happens when it fails in a particular operational environment and whether its decisions can be audited afterward.

Statistical AI systems can fail differently from traditional software, Chapa said, including producing substantially different outputs from relatively small changes in inputs. More complex systems can also make it difficult to reconstruct how a particular recommendation was produced after the fact.

He called for greater AI education across the military, including specialized training for personnel working with targeting and intelligence systems.

Witnesses on Wednesday also pointed to a larger accountability problem: determining what happens when an AI-assisted decision results in civilian harm.

The Defense Department established its Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response Action Plan in 2022, including a Civilian Protection Center of Excellence intended to serve as a hub for analysis and training. Federal law requires the Pentagon to operate the center.

But a Defense Department inspector general review released in May assessed the department’s implementation of the civilian-harm framework and found problems including the loss or reassignment of personnel, the end of funding for a civilian-harm data-management platform and the failure of a senior steering committee to continue meeting.

That matters in the case of AI because, as Klasing noted, the military currently has limited ability to determine whether AI may contribute to improper targeting of civilians.

On the first day of the U.S.-Iran war, a Tomahawk cruise missile struck Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school in Minab, southern Iran. At least 168 people were killed — more than 100 of them under the age of 12, according to UN and Iranian officials.

The school building sat fewer than 100 yards from a long-time Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps naval installation and was previously located within the IRGC compound perimeter until a wall appeared between 2013 and 2016, according to an analysis of satellite imagery by Amnesty International .

By the time the U.S. and Israel launched their first strikes on Feb. 28, the school had been established several years prior. It was active on social media and had its own website, a Reuters investigation found.

More than 120 House Democrats sent a letter to the Pentagon on March 12 , demanding clarity on whether artificial intelligence, “including the use of the Maven Smart System, [was] used to identify the Shajareh Tayyebeh school as a target.”

U.S. military investigators in the wake of the incident stated that the strike was likely carried out by U.S. forces. The Pentagon, however, has still not released its investigative findings.

Klasing proposed adding information about AI involvement to the Pentagon’s annual civilian-casualty reports required under Section 1057 of the National Defense Authorization Act. The existing reporting requirement calls for information about civilian casualty mitigation efforts and investigations, but does not specifically require the department to identify whether AI contributed to an incident.

Steve Feldstein, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said the Pentagon should collect data from military operations and conduct after-action reviews to determine whether AI-assisted systems accurately identified intended targets and whether errors contributed to civilian casualties.

“A bigger question is to what extent is the Pentagon collecting data and verifying the target accuracy of all these 1000s of strikes?” Feldstein said.

Feldstein also cautioned against treating AI itself as the source of every potential problem. AI can be used to help verify intelligence, detect changes in imagery and prioritize defensive responses to threats such as drones and ballistic missiles.

But if a human-influenced system is built around assumptions that certain demographic traits make someone a lawful target, Mysyshyn said, AI would not correct that underlying premise.

Feldstein similarly pointed to the rules humans establish before an AI system is used. If commanders determine that a particular level of civilian harm is acceptable in pursuit of a military objective, he said, the machine is operating within a human-defined framework.

The challenge is particularly acute when systems operate faster than people can meaningfully assess recommendations.

The commission opened Wednesday’s hearing with an example from Iraq. In 2004, Army squad leader Nick Ellison encountered two young men firing a machine gun from a car during a census patrol in Kirkuk.

Ellison made eye contact with one of the men, saw panic and ordered his soldiers to hold fire. The men turned out to be brothers of a newly married groom, and the gunfire was celebratory.

Mysyshyn said testing should examine bias, reliability, civilian protection, realistic time pressure, whether operators can interrupt systems and whether decisions can be traced throughout an AI system’s lifecycle.

Chapa said some AI systems may be difficult to audit after the fact, while Deborah Brown of Human Rights Watch said information about military AI use has often emerged through investigative reporting and whistleblowers rather than government disclosures.

The growing challenge, according to witnesses, is no longer making a machine pull a trigger, but whether the human who approves the trigger pull has enough time, information and authority to make a meaningful choice before disaster.

Military Times reporter Katie Livingstone contributed to this report.

Natalie Oliverio is an independent journalist and Navy veteran who covers military and veterans’ issues. Drawing on her experience as a talent executive and mentor, she writes about the policies, people and programs shaping the military community.

items.title: How the Space Force Is Preparing for Its New Moving Target Missions
items.author: Courtney Albon
items.summary: As the Space Force prepares to field new fleets of satellites that can track moving targets in the air and on the ground, it’s working to ensure it has the organizational structures in place to onboard and operate those systems. The post How the Space Force Is Preparing for Its New Moving Target Missions appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —As the Space Force prepares to field new fleets of satellites that can track moving targets in the air and on the ground, it’s working to ensure it has the organizational structures in place to onboard and operate those systems.

The U.S. military has long relied on large aircraft like the E-3 Sentry to track airborne targets, but leaders have become increasingly concerned that those platforms are vulnerable to long-range weapons. In recent years, the Space Force and the National Reconnaissance Office have been working to leverage satellites for the mission, an approach leaders expect will make the capability more resilient against adversaries’ anti-access/aerial-denial systems.

While the effort is still nascent and there’s much to prove about the ability of a satellite constellation to provide timely, clear tracks of moving targets like drones, missiles, and aircraft, the Pentagon has made some strides to demonstrate viability.

The NRO has launched some ground moving target indicator, or GMTI, satellites as part of its multimission proliferated low-Earth orbit constellation . And the head of Combat Forces Command, Lt. Gen. Gregory Gagnon, told reporters Sept. 16 that the Space Force expects to launch a new GMTI capability called Resilient Radar System-Ground in the next year or two. Those spacecraft are being built by Northrop Grumman, he said during a briefing at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.

The Space Force is also on the verge of launching its first space-based air moving target indicator, or AMTI , satellites. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Sept. 14 the spacecraft would launch later this month. Acquisition officials have declined to detail how many satellites will launch or provide a date for the mission. The only Space Force launch scheduled for this month, according to Spaceflight Now’s public launch listing , is USSF-259, a classified payload slated to lift off Sept. 16 from Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif., on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.

The service awarded SpaceX a contract in May worth up to $4.2 billion to begin building out the AMTI constellation. The company is one of 12 vendors selected to compete for space-based AMTI contracts.

Col. Ryan Frazier, the Space Force’s portfolio acquisition executive for space-based sensing and targeting, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in July the service expects to have a “usable” space-based AMTI capability by 2028 , noting that those satellites will be a first step toward an on-orbit targeting capability but not a full solution.

“Is it everything the joint force requires? I think that will probably extend beyond ‘28,” Frazier said. “But we are going to have capabilities they don’t have today. … We’ll be able to do things that are high-value or value-added. We won’t be able to do them everywhere all the time.”

Frazier told reporters Sept. 15 that the first space-based AMTI deliveries will provide a baseline for the rest of the architecture, allowing the Space Force to fine-tune and calibrate its satellites and processing algorithms.

“There’s a broader architecture that we need to build out for the joint force to be able to close on its long-range kill chain missions,” he said. “There’s how you battle manage with that data, how you apply the processing algorithms, get that data to the weapons and the shooters that you need, and the time latencies that requires.”

As the acquisition community develops and demonstrates new systems to perform the mission, the Space Force is standing up the operational units that will manage them. On July 31, CFC activated the 77th Surveillance Squadron within Space Delta 7. The role of the 77th is to take the intelligence collected by those AMTI and GMTI satellites and deliver it to decision-makers who will determine whether to attack a particular target.

“They will use information provided from the space layer, fuse that with other sources of information and intelligence, and make decisions about weapons engagement,” Gagnon said.

Meanwhile, U.S. Space Command is working with other combatant commands and the intelligence community to craft a concept of operations for the new mission area—a document that will describe how military operators will put the system to use. SPACECOM Commander Gen. Stephen Whiting told reporters Sept. 16 his team is working with the Space Force and the NRO to solidify a plan to transition those satellites to the command once they’re deemed ready for operations.

“This will be new and different as we elevate AMTI and GMTI to space,” Whiting said. “But we do have decades of lessons learned from AMTI and GMTI in other domains.”

items.title: Lockheed’s New Modular JASSM Offers Swappable Noses and Launch Options
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: Lockheed Martin has unveiled its concept for a modular version of one of the Air Force’s main air-to-ground cruise missiles, opening up a range of possible upgrades and uses for the weapon. The post Lockheed’s New Modular JASSM Offers Swappable Noses and Launch Options appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —Lockheed Martin has unveiled its concept for a modular version of one of the Air Force’s main air-to-ground cruise missiles, opening up a range of possible upgrades and uses for the weapon.

Lockheed revealed the AGM-158 FLEX airframe, based on the Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missile, at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference this week. The airframe has a removable nose cone to let users swap in different sensors and a reconfigurable tail for different launch options.

“The AGM-158 FLEX airframe concept was driven by a strategic need to keep pace with rapidly evolving threats, insert emerging technologies quickly, manage obsolescence, and provide, at scale, a cost-effective missile family that can be repurposed for a wide range of missions while delivering timely, relevant capability to the warfighter,” a Lockheed Martin spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine via email.

The spokesperson did not answer questions about whether the Air Force has contracted or ordered the FLEX or what stage of development the project is in. Lockheed did say in a release that it has invested $35 million of its own money on the idea, based on what the firm called “a demand from our customers to have increased options.”

The Air Force has shown interest in modular munitions before—in January 2025, the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center published a notice to industry seeking technology to allow for its Extended Range Attack Munition project to have modular parts for its subcomponents. The ERAM is also a standoff cruise missile, which the Air Force rercently developed as a low-cost option to bolster its stockpiles.

Indeed, the Air Force and the rest of the U.S. military are keen to build up their weapons stocks after using thousands to strike Iran during the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The U.S. used 1,100 JASSMs over just the first 39 days of the conflict, according to an analysis from the Center for Strategic and International Studies in April.

Given that high usage and demand, the Air Force plans to significantly ramp up production of JASSM and its Long-Range Anti-Ship variant—and Lockheed sees FLEX as a way to further bolster the stockpile with more options.

The concept “will allow customers to quickly integrate capabilities,” Lockheed’s release states, and allow JASSM to be configured for surface, sub-surface, and ground launch options.

The air-launched version will remain compatible with all current and future JASSM and LRASM air-launched platforms.

Size options include a 206-inch extreme range option, the same size as the existing JASSM-XR, and a 168-inch extended range version, the same size as the JASSM-ER.

Both are built to give users “significantly increased standoff attack range.”

The weapon could feature in the latest iteration of a yearslong effort known as “Rapid Dragon,” which has now shifted to become “Dragon Cart,” a project to launch cruise missiles from palletized loads dropped from the ramps of transport and cargo aircraft such as the C-130 and C-17.

“As Rapid Dragon transitions into a Dragon Cart program of record, it becomes a viable deployment platform for a variety of Air Force munitions, both in inventory and in development,” the Lockheed spokesperson wrote. “While we can’t offer specific examples today, Lockheed Martin does consider all potential launch platforms in maturing munition offerings.”

items.title: The Only Air Force Fighter Pilot in Congress Wants ‘Wingmen to Come Join Me’
items.author: Greg Hadley
items.summary: When the 119th Congress took office in January 2025, it counted a record seven former Navy SEALs among its members—and just one former Air Force fighter pilot. Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas), a former F-15 and F-22 pilot, says that must change to help the Air Force get the resources it needs to recapitalize. The post The Only Air Force Fighter Pilot in Congress Wants ‘Wingmen to Come Join Me’ appeared first on Air &
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —When the 119th Congress took office in January 2025, it counted a record seven former Navy SEALs among its members—and just one former Air Force fighter pilot.

Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas), an Air Force veteran who flew F-15 and F-22 fighters, says that needs to change so the Air Force gets the resources it needs to recapitalize its rapidly aging air fleet.

“I am the only fifth-generation pilot in Congress,” Pfluger said Sept. 16 at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference. “I need some wingmen to come join me. … God bless my Navy SEAL friends, and they are dear friends, but we’ve got a lot of them in Congress. What we don’t have is a lot of air and space expertise.”

Indeed, among the 96 veterans now in Congress, just 15 are Air Force veterans: only 15.6 percent. By comparison, there are 45 Army vets, 24 Navy vets, and 12 former Marines. The Space Force isn’t seven years old yet, but no former Space Force Guardians have been elected to Congress.

Of the 15 former Airmen on Capitol Hill, Pfluger is not the only aviator—Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) flew on the EC-130H and RC-135, Rep. Troy Downing (R-Mont.) was in combat search and rescue, and Rep. Zach Nunn (R-Iowa) was an airborne intelligence officer.

But there are no other USAF fighter pilots. In 2022, Pfluger started the “Mach 1” caucus with three former Navy fighter pilots. Four years and two elections later, the Mach 1 caucus has gone from four to three members: Pfluger, Rep. Jake Ellzey (R-Texas), and Rep. Scott Franklin (R-Fla.).

With such small numbers, Pfluger said, it’s harder for the Air Force to “tell its story.”

“What I have done in Congress is try to educate my colleagues on what the Department of the Air Force does and why we, as a department, are really carrying the load in each of the conflicts—whether it’s Epic Fury, Midnight Hammer, Absolute Resolve, or any of the previous conflicts, the Department of the Air Force has been there every single time,” Pfluger said.

Airpower, Pfluger said, is uniquely capable of providing strategic effects. But modernization—and the resources that go along with it—is desperately needed.

We … need the help to make the case that while we are the oldest and the smallest, it’s not too late. We can recapitalize,” Pfluger said, lamenting that budget increases cannot be split evenly among the services if the Air Force is to shoulder much of the operational load.

More Airmen in Congress would help him make the case to other lawmakers, Pfluger said. For now, he gets help from Representatives and Senators who represent key Air Force installations. But he also urged Air Force leaders to make their case to Congress.

“We need Air Force leaders to be bold,” Pfluger said. “We need you to be bold to tell the truth, to say we’re underfunded.”

Multiyear Procurement

While the Air Force needs to make its case to Congress, Congress can help the Air Force by not only providing more resources, but making those resources more consistent.

Pentagon officials frequently decry the effects of continuing resolutions and government shutdowns when lawmakers fail to pass appropriations on time.

A more “predictable environment” is important, Pfluger agreed. One way to do that is multiyear procurement authorities—letting the Pentagon award contracts for multiple years instead of being reliant on annual cycles. Congress must approve any and all programs for which Pentagon wants to use multiyear procurement.

Defense officials say multiyear procurement saves the government money by locking in lower prices and helps industry by providing a stable demand signal. In the past, lawmakers have raised concerns about oversight, but they have grown increasingly open to granting more authorities.

Congress has already implemented multiyear procurement for a range of munitions programs, but members of the House and Senate Armed Services Committees have voted to authorize it for the F-35 and F-15EX as part of the 2027 defense policy bill. That bill is still pending, but Pfluger projected confidence that expanded multiyear procurement authorities are coming.

“I’m very convinced that we’re very close to getting some of these things accomplished,” Pfluger said

items.title: New AMC Boss Open to Unmanned Next-Gen Tanker
items.author: Matthew Cox
items.summary: The new head of Air Mobility Command said Sept. 16 he wants to explore an unmanned option for the service’s next-generation aerial refueling system. The post New AMC Boss Open to Unmanned Next-Gen Tanker appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —The new head of Air Mobility Command said Sept. 16 he wants to explore an unmanned option for the service’s next-generation aerial refueling system.

As the service pursues its first fleet of semi-autonomous Collaborative Combat Aircraft , Lt. Gen. Daniel Tulley said he is open to looking at emerging technologies for a future unmanned or optionally manned large aerial refueling aircraft. The service is preparing to sign a deal for 75 additional KC-46 Pegasus tankers, but it continues to search for a long-term answer to replacing its Eisenhower-era KC-135 Stratotanker s, the bulk of today’s tanker fleet.

To field a next-generation tanker in the mid-2030s, the Air Force is pursuing an analysis of alternatives, looking at everything from an innovative blended wing-body aircraft to more KC-46s to a stealthy and possibly uncrewed refueling platform.

“Thinking beyond the current KC-46 buy and the program extension, whatever that next tanker looks like—our advanced tanker system—it’s got to be connected. It’s got to be able to defend itself, but it begs the question: does it need to be manned? Could it be optionally manned? It could be autonomous, or is there a family of solutions maybe that would answer that question?” Tulley, who took command of AMC in early August, told reporters at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.

“I do not believe that it has to be a manned future air refueling solution,” Tulley said. “I think you’re seeing that with the MQ-25 and the Navy’s work,” Tulley added, referring to the Navy’s development of the uncrewed MQ-25 from Boeing, an unmanned tanker capable of transferring 14,000 pounds of fuel to aircraft like the F/A-18 Super Hornet and the F-35 at a distance of 500 miles from a carrier in highly contested airspace.

That airplane is much smaller than Air Force requirements, however; a KC-46 can carry 212,000 pounds of fuel, more than 15 times the capacity of the MQ-25.

Solving that problem is what Tulley is after. “How do we, the U.S. Air Force, bring that to bear in scope, scale, and range?” he asked. “An optionally manned or an unmanned tanker at the ranges we need to operate at is a very large aircraft.”

Currently, the Air Force is not yet “employing fully autonomous large aircraft, but the technology I would say [is] … rapidly getting there,” Tulley said.

Boeing’s large civilian airliners can take off with very little help, fly on a programed route, and land with autopilot, “but we don’t employ [aircraft] that way,” Tulley said.

The market for autonomy in large aircraft is a military market, so “establishing the requirement and then supporting the requirement with the right technology” will be key, he said.

“There are some companies out there who have offered to develop things where they can bring a carry-on kit on KC-135s and other aircraft,” he said. “But we haven’t seen them test those successfully.”

Meanwhile, the Air Force and Boeing unveiled an agreement in mid-May to resolve critical deficiencies with the Pegasus that currently stand in the way of the service signing a pending contract for 75 additional KC-46s. The service is also working to add connectivity and active defense systems on both the KC-135 and the newer KC-46.

“We are going to be recapitalizing tankers for decades, and in the interim, the same dedication to bringing on new platforms is necessary to sustain those that we have,” Maj. Gen. Gerald Donohue, deputy commander of Air Mobility Command, said during the conference. “The last KC-135 pilot has not been born.”

items.title: Blood, Sweat and Stairs: Goodfellow honors 9/11 first responders
items.author: SrA Renee Nicole Finona
items.summary: Firefighters climbed five stories carrying 42-pound packs, advanced hose lines and dragged a 185-pound mannequin as part of the 14th annual Blood, Sweat and Stairs event, Sept. 12. Hosted by the 312th Training Squadron at the Louis F. Garland Department of War Fire Academy, the event honored the first responders who answered the call during the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks while challenging participants through a memorial run and firefighter combat challenge.
items.body: GOODFELLOW AIR FORCE BASE, Texas -- Firefighters climbed five stories carrying 42-pound packs, advanced hose lines and dragged a 185-pound mannequin as part of the 14th annual Blood, Sweat and Stairs event, Sept. 12. Hosted by the 312th Training Squadron at the Louis F. Garland Department of War Fire Academy, the event honored the first responders who answered the call during the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks while challenging participants through a memorial run and firefighter combat challenge. The event began with the 5K Memorial Run, giving participants an opportunity to remember those who lost their lives during the response to the attacks. Following the run, teams gathered for the firefighter combat challenge, a series of physically demanding events designed to test strength, endurance and teamwork. “Yesterday, we remembered 9/11 through a bunch of different activities, through a ceremony,” said Lt. Col. Benjamin Shearer, 312th TRS commander. “This morning we continue to remember 9/11, just with a little bit of a different flavor.” The combat challenge began with a high-rise climb. The first competitor carried a 42-pound high-rise pack to the top of the academy's five-story Soldiers/Sailors, Airmen and Marines Tower before tagging the next teammate. Teams then progressed through additional events that included hoisting equipment, a Keiser force machine, navigating a 100-foot serpentine course and advancing a hose line to engage a target and a mannequin drag. While the event tested competitors physically, its purpose extended beyond the competition. Blood, Sweat and Stairs connected remembrance with the demands of the firefighting profession, highlighting the preparation, physical readiness and teamwork required of those who respond when others need help. The event brought together firefighters, commanders, senior leaders, first sergeants and members of the Goodfellow community to support the competitors and recognize the significance of the day. Twenty-five years after the 9/11 terrorist attacks, the event provided another opportunity for the Goodfellow community to honor the first responders who demonstrated courage and commitment in the face of unimaginable danger.

items.title: 2026 Fort McCoy Retiree Appreciation Day honors service, strengthens retiree connections
items.author: Scott Sturkol
items.summary: Military service may eventually bring a service member’s active-duty or Reserve career to an end, but the connection to the military does not end with retirement.
items.body: Military service may eventually bring a service member’s active-duty or Reserve career to an end, but the connection to the military does not end with retirement. That connection was highlighted Sept. 11, 2026, when Fort McCoy hosted its annual Retiree Appreciation Day, bringing military retirees, veterans, spouses and members of the military community together for information, fellowship and an opportunity to stay connected with the services and benefits available to them. The annual event, organized by the Fort McCoy Soldier for Life Retirement Services Office within the Directorate of Human Resources, was held in building 905. Fort McCoy Retirement Services Officer Nicholas Gimson continues to lead the installation’s retirement-services effort and has been instrumental in organizing recent Retiree Appreciation Days. The purpose of the event is straightforward: bring retirees together while providing them with current information about the benefits and services they have earned through military service. Fort McCoy’s Retirement Services Office describes Retiree Appreciation Day as an annual September event featuring a morning session with guest speakers from organizations that affect military retirees' lives, followed by a benefits fair with representatives from military retiree and veteran-related organizations. For Gimson, that combination of information and personal connection is an important part of serving the Fort McCoy retiree community. “The ultimate goal of a Retiree Appreciation Day is to bring together military retirees and give them an opportunity to receive some of the most up-to-date information on the benefits they are entitled to with a seminar setting,” Gimson said in discussing previous Fort McCoy RAD events. The event is open not only to military retirees, but also to those transitioning into retirement and their spouses. A continuing connection to service Retiree Appreciation Day has become an annual Fort McCoy tradition, but its format has evolved over the years to better serve the retiree community. The 2022 RAD was the first Fort McCoy Retiree Appreciation Day since 2019 and drew more than 300 attendees. The return of the event provided an opportunity for retirees and family members to reconnect with one another while receiving information about benefits and services. The 2023 event also drew more than 300 military retirees and family members. That event featured a prayer breakfast, briefings on subjects including TRICARE and Social Security, a Wisconsin Department of Veterans Affairs presentation, county veterans service officers, a benefits expo and other activities. Attendees could also visit the Fort McCoy Commemorative Area and History Center. The 2023 event demonstrated another important aspect of RAD: it is not simply a series of presentations. It provides an opportunity for retirees to reconnect with the installation and with the Army community. In 2023, nearly 100 RAD attendees visited the Fort McCoy Commemorative Area, where they toured the History Center, Veterans Memorial Plaza and Equipment Park and learned more about the installation's history and heritage. Information retirees can use The benefits and services available to military retirees can change over time, making opportunities such as RAD important for keeping retirees informed. Fort McCoy’s Retirement Services Office provides assistance to Soldiers and their families preparing for retirement as well as retired Soldiers, surviving spouses and families. The office provides counseling concerning retirement rights, benefits and entitlements, Survivor Benefit Plan information and Reserve Component Survivor Benefit Plan counseling. It also helps keep retirees informed about changes in laws and benefits. The Fort McCoy RSO also offers pre-retirement and Survivor Benefit Plan briefings, either in group settings or individually. RAD brings many of those resources together in one location. Past events have included representatives from the Fort McCoy Retirement Services Office, TRICARE, transition assistance, Military OneSource, county veterans service offices and other organizations serving military retirees and veterans. The format gives retirees an opportunity to ask questions directly and learn about resources they may not otherwise encounter in one place. More than benefits While information is an important part of Retiree Appreciation Day, the event also recognizes something larger — the continuing value of the military retiree community. At the 2023 event, Fort McCoy Garrison Commander Col. Stephen Messenger thanked retirees and their families for their service and emphasized the importance of the support systems surrounding military service. “Everyone needs a support system,” Messenger said during the event. “And the military provides that through these forums, the Retirement Services Office, and all the benefits that come with it.” That support extends beyond the individual who served. Military families are an important part of the retiree community, having supported Soldiers through deployments, permanent changes of station, training, long hours and the many demands associated with military life. That is why Fort McCoy RAD events are open to retirees, those preparing to retire and spouses. A tradition that continues Recent Retiree Appreciation Days have also demonstrated how Fort McCoy organizations work together to support the retiree community. In 2024, for example, the Fort McCoy Commissary held a special sidewalk sale during RAD, providing retirees and family members another opportunity to participate in installation activities while attending the event. That year’s RAD served 155 retirees, veterans and spouses, according to Gimson. “Retiree Appreciation Day was a tremendous success,” Gimson said following the 2024 event. “We had the pleasure of serving 155 retirees, veterans, and spouses. This year, we welcomed several new community partners, and the feedback from attendees was overwhelmingly positive.” Gimson said many attendees expressed interest in having additional time and events available during future RADs. The 2024 event also continued the tradition of opening the Fort McCoy Commemorative Area to RAD attendees. Nearly 60 retirees and family members visited the area to explore Fort McCoy and Army history. The combination of information, fellowship and access to Fort McCoy resources has helped make RAD an important annual event for the installation's retiree community. Serving those who served Fort McCoy’;s commitment to retirees extends beyond one day each year. The installation’s Retirement Services Office is available throughout the year to help retirees and their families understand and navigate their military benefits. The office is located in building 2187 and provides walk-in service, although appointments are recommended. The office can be reached at 502-898-3716. Fort McCoy’s motto beginning in 2026 is “Training the Total Force and Shaping the Future since 1909.” The installation’s mission: “Fort McCoy strengthens Total Force Readiness by serving as a training center, Mobilization Force Generation Installation, and Strategic Support Area enabling warfighter lethality to deploy, fight, and win our nation’s wars.” And Fort McCoy’s vision is, “To be the premier training center supporting the most capable, combat-ready, and lethal armed forces.” Located in the heart of the upper Midwest, Fort McCoy is the only U.S. Army installation in Wisconsin. The installation has provided support and facilities for the field and classroom training of more than 100,000 military personnel from all services nearly every year since 1984. Learn more about Fort McCoy online athttps://home.army.mil/mccoy, on Facebook by searching “ftmccoy,” on Flickr at https://www.flickr.com/photos/fortmccoywi, and on X (formerly Twitter) by searching “usagmccoy.” Also try downloading the My Army Post app to your smartphone and set “Fort McCoy” or another installation as your preferred base. Fort McCoy is also part of Army’s Installation Management Command where “We Are The Army’s Home.”

items.title: Spirit of 9/11 remains alive through remembrance
items.author: Laisa Leao
items.summary: To honor American unity, sacrifice and resilience, while underscoring the enduring need for national vigilance, the 412th Test Wing Fire and Emergency Services team hosted a 9/11 remembrance event at Edwards Air Force Base, California, Sept. 11.
items.body:
To honor American unity, sacrifice and resilience, while underscoring the enduring need for national vigilance, the 412th Test Wing Fire and Emergency Services team hosted a 9/11 remembrance event at Edwards Air Force Base, California, Sept. 11.

Senior Airman Daniel Halicho, Senior Airman Ethan Wright and Staff Sgt. Jesse Pueschel, firefighters with the 412th Test Wing Fire and Emergency Services, march during a 9/11 remembrance ceremony at Edwards Air Force Base, California, Sept. 11. In 2001, Halicho and Wright were not yet born, and Pueschel was just a child, but they joined fellow first responders to honor the sacrifice of the 343 firefighters who died in the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. (U.S. Air Force photo by Lindsey Gordon)

The event featured a memorial walk-run and ceremony highlighted by remarks from Mike Wilbur, a retired Fire Department of New York firefighter who served on World Trade Center search and recovery teams after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.

“After a few days of working on the pile, I was able to go home and see my family," said Wilbur. "One of the hardest things I had to do was gather them in the living room and tell them I’m ok but I have to go back.”

Mike Wilbur, a retired Fire Department of New York firefighter, speaks about his time working on search and recovery teams at the World Trade Center site following the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, during a remembrance event at Edwards Air Force Base, California, Sept. 11. (U.S. Air Force photo by Lindsey Gordon)

A quarter-century after the 2001 terrorist attacks, an entire generation of Americans has grown up without firsthand memories of that morning. Yet history endures through documentary footage, classroom instruction and personal recollections shared by those who lived through the tragedy.

On that morning, 19 hijackers took control of four commercial jetliners to strike symbols of American strength and democracy. Two planes destroyed the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in New York. A third struck the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia. The fourth, United Airlines Flight 93, crashed into an open field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers and crew members fought back against the hijackers, preventing an attack on the U.S. Capitol or the White House.

The attacks claimed nearly 3,000 lives, including passengers, crew members, civilian workers inside the targeted buildings and hundreds of first responders who rushed into danger to save others.

Decades later, Sept. 11 stands as both a solemn reminder of national vigilance and an enduring tribute to the bravery and resilience that followed.

items.title: Never Forget: Honoring 25 Years Since 9/11
items.author: A1C Maria Mota and A1C Brayden Pridgen
items.summary: Twenty-five years after the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, we continue to honor the lives lost and pay tribute to the courage of those who answered the call.
items.body:
Twenty-five years after the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, we continue to honor the lives lost and pay tribute to the courage of those who answered the call.

The community of San Angelo united to honor those lost at the annual memorial service held at the city’s 9/11 monument, Sept. 11, 2026.

During the ceremony, U.S. Air Force Col. Matthew Norton, 17th Training Wing commander, spoke on the lasting impact of the 9/11 attacks and how the events affected the nation, the military and his own path of service.

“That same calling shaped the lives of thousands of fellow service members,” said Norton. “Those who were already wearing the cloth of our nation, and the countless patriots that raised their right hand in the days and years that followed. Every single day of our service has been defined by what has transpired across New York City, at the Pentagon, and in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania.”

As the service continued, San Angelo’s leaders expressed gratitude for the community’s continued support of those who serve and defend the nation.

“I am so thankful for this community that continues, year in and year out, to remember the sacrifices of our first responders and military and 3,000-plus victims,” said U.S. Rep. August Pfluger. “Let us never forget that freedom is never free.”

Later that day, members of Goodfellow Air Force Base showed respect to the fallen heroes of 9/11 through a remembrance ceremony held at the Louis F. Garland Department of War Fire Academy.

“343, as we know, because that's a big number, were firefighters. 23, New York Police Department. 37 Port Authority police officers, ” said retired Chief Master Sgt. Anthony Robinson.

The ceremony commemorated the 403 first responders who lost their lives while responding to the attacks.

Speakers at the event mentioned that following the first attack, first responders immediately assisted those in need, unsure of the risk that presented itself. Through blurry vision from smoke and debris, the goal was clear: to save as many people as possible.

The terrorist attacks remain engraved in the nation's history. The memory of those brave heroes and their sacrifices continues to influence how first responders are trained, helping ensure they are prepared to protect their communities.

“Twenty-five years ago, the world changed in an instant,” said Norton. “Today, we gather in solemn remembrance of the 2,977 innocent lives stolen from us in the deadliest terrorist attack on American soil.”

First responders from the Goodfellow Medical Group, 17th Security Forces Squadron and 312th Training Squadron recited prayers to honor the memory of those lost.

As the ceremony concluded, guests were encouraged to place a name on the Board of Honor, honoring the immense sacrifice and courage of those who responded to the attacks.

“Twenty-five years later, we remember, we honor, and we stand resolute in our conviction. ‘No day shall erase you from the memory of time,’” said Norton.

items.title: myAuth transition brings new login process to Fort Hood military community
items.author: Rodney Jackson
items.summary: Carl R. Darnall Army Medical Center encourages members of the Fort Hood military community to prepare for changes to the way they access the MHS GENESIS Patient Portal and other Department of Defense health care and benefits systems as they transition to myAuth.
items.body:
Carl R. Darnall Army Medical Center encourages members of the Fort Hood military community to prepare for changes to the way they access the MHS GENESIS Patient Portal and other Department of Defense health care and benefits systems as they transition to myAuth.

The Department of Defense is replacing its legacy DS Logon system with myAuth, a modernized authentication system designed to provide beneficiaries with a more secure and streamlined way to access their health care and benefits information online. The transition is occurring in phases, with some DoD systems already using myAuth while others, including the MHS GENESIS Patient Portal, are scheduled to transition.

The MHS GENESIS Patient Portal, the DoD’s single electronic health record portal, is scheduled to transition on Sept. 23. Beneficiaries should create or update their myAuth account before the transition.

The myAuth information page at https://myaccess.dmdc.osd.mil/identitymanagement/help/myauth.htm provides account instructions, frequently asked questions and transition updates. Users can also access their DS Logon account through the page. What should beneficiaries do now?

Set up a myAuth account now. Beneficiaries who still have an active DS Logon can use their DS Logon username and password to verify their identity during the myAuth registration process.

Keep your DS Logon information available for now. Some DoD health care systems are still transitioning, so beneficiaries may continue to encounter DS Logon on websites that have not yet moved to myAuth.

Don't wait until you urgently need medical information. Establishing myAuth ahead of the transition can help prevent access problems when additional health care platforms move over.

Make sure your information is current in DEERS. Accurate beneficiary information helps support access to DoD health care and benefits systems.

Use official websites only. Beneficiaries should access myAuth through official DoD/TRICARE websites and be cautious of unsolicited messages requesting login information.

If you don't have a DS Logon, don't assume you're stuck. Depending on the beneficiary's circumstances, myAuth provides other identity-verification options, including CAC-based verification.

What to expect MHS GENESIS is the DoD's electronic health record portal, allowing beneficiaries to view health information, manage appointments, request prescription refills and securely communicate with their health care teams.

After the transition, users will see myAuth as the portal's login option. myAuth supports Common Access Card authentication or a username and password with secure multifactor authentication.

Seeing a new login screen does not indicate a problem with an account. Beneficiaries should follow the instructions displayed on the portal when logging in.

The transition will occur in phases across DoD and TRICARE platforms. Several websites, including milConnect, ID Card Office Online and the TRICARE East and West Region beneficiary portals, already use myAuth. Other platforms will transition in the coming months.

Beneficiaries should use only official DoD or TRICARE websites when accessing their accounts and avoid unfamiliar links requesting login information.

For technical assistance with myAuth or DS Logon, contact the Defense Manpower Data Center, which manages both authentication systems and can be reached at 800-368-3665, 800-477-8227 or by visiting the myAuth information page.

Additional information is available on the official TRICARE myAuth information page at https://tricare.mil/GettingCare/VirtualHealth/SecurePatientPortal/SecureLogin/myAuth? .

Preparing now can help ensure continued access to MHS GENESIS when the new login system takes effect Sept. 23.

items.title: NCG-1 Announces FY27 CPO Pinning
items.author: Gabriel Perez
items.summary: NCG-1 hosted the Fiscal Year 2027 Chief Petty Officer (CPO) Pinning Ceremony at Naval Base Ventura County (NBVC), Port Hueneme, Calif., Sept. 16, 2026.
items.body:
PORT HUENEME, Calif. (September 16, 2026) – Naval Construction Group (NCG) 1 hosted the Fiscal Year 2027 Chief Petty Officer (CPO) Pinning Ceremony at Naval Base Ventura County (NBVC), Port Hueneme, Calif., Sept. 16, 2026.

The ceremony marked the culmination of a demanding six-week training period, during which the selectees underwent rigorous leadership challenges and team-building exercises to prepare them for their new roles in the Chiefs Mess. The event celebrated the promotion of Sailors who will now wear the coveted anchor collar devices.

Capt. Andrew Litteral, commodore, NCG-1, hosted the event. The guest speaker, retired Command Master Chief Corey Stevens, addressed the new Chiefs and their families.

CMDCM Stevens said, “Remember this: the Chiefs Mess is perfect, the chiefs are not. Also keep in mind that Chiefs are troops too and we are not invincible.” Stevens concluded his speech with, “Chiefs anchor up, knuckle down, and always remember since 1893, Navy Chief, Navy Pride!”

Capt. Litteral then took the podium to deliver remarks to the selectees and their families.

“As Chiefs in the Seabees, you are the keepers of the ‘Can Do’ spirit,” said Capt. Litteral, “From this day forward, you are no longer evaluated by what you can build or fix with your own hands, you are evaluated by the readiness, the safety, the proficiency, and the courage of the Sailors you lead.”

Capt. Litteral finished his speech with an encouraging message to the soon-to-be pinned Chiefs, “Stand tall today, ready to build, ready to fight, and ready to lead, welcome to the Chiefs Mess.”

The following NCG-1 personnel were pinned to Chief Petty Officer: U.S. Navy Chief Yeoman Ashley Mcmillan U.S. Navy Chief Equipment Operator Christian Rivera U.S. Navy Chief Engineering Aide Devin Watts U.S. Marine Corps Gunnery Sgt. Tyler Brooks U.S. Navy Chief Yeoman Jacqueline Evans U.S. Navy Chief Gunner’s Mate Angela Haley U.S. Navy Chief Construction Electrician Mike Johnson U.S. Navy Chief Steelworker Lizeth Cruzjuarez U.S. Marine Corps Gunnery Sgt. Matthew Barrett U.S. Navy Chief Builder Aaron Brown U.S. Navy Chief Equipment Operator Thomas Dahlke U.S. Navy Chief Construction Mechanic Robert Norton U.S. Navy Chief Hospital Corpsman Bobby Whited U.S. Navy Chief Construction Mechanic Jan Lumboy U.S. Navy Chief Construction Electrician Claudia Mendez U.S. Navy Chief Construction Electrician German Valdez U.S. Navy Chief Builder Ryan Hlavac U.S. Navy Chief Construction Mechanic Keith Roman U.S. Navy Chief Builder Colt Hawkins U.S. Navy Chief Construction Electrician Travis Mitchell U.S. Navy Chief Personnel Specialist Kellee Smith U.S. Navy Chief Builder Eric Erkan U.S. Navy Chief Builder Dan Kvaley U.S. Navy Chief Builder Megan Pringle U.S. Navy Chief Construction Electrician Derek Drummond

The ceremony concluded with the reading of the CPO Creed, a time-honored tradition that reaffirms the commitment and responsibilities of a Chief Petty Officer. Friends, family and mentors pinned the new anchors on each Chief, underscoring the vital role of a strong support system in a Sailor's career.

NCG-1 leads and manages all Naval Construction Force units in the Pacific Fleet, providing adaptive expeditionary construction and engineering capabilities to support fleet and joint force commanders.

items.title: Marine Forces Reserve Hosts the 2026 Senior Personnel Administration Training Symposium at Marine Corps Support Facility New Orleans
items.author: LCpl Nalanie Davila
items.summary: NEW ORLEANS — Marine Forces Reserve personnel administrators gathered for the Fiscal Year 2026 Senior Personnel Administration Training Symposium at Marine Corps Support Facility New Orleans, Sept. 15–17, 2026, bringing together administrative leaders from across the force to strengthen proficiency, address administrative challenges and improve support to Reserve Marines.
items.body:
NEW ORLEANS — Marine Forces Reserve personnel administrators gathered for the Fiscal Year 2026 Senior Personnel Administration Training Symposium at Marine Corps Support Facility New Orleans, Sept. 15–17, 2026, bringing together administrative leaders from across the force to strengthen proficiency, address administrative challenges and improve support to Reserve Marines.

The annual symposium serves as a premier administrative training evolution for Marine Forces Reserve, providing active component, Active Reserve personnel officers, administrative chiefs and Headquarters Marine Corps representatives an opportunity to synchronize policies, share best techniques and engage directly with subject matter experts.

U.S. Marine Corps Col. Catherine Sumruld, assistant chief of staff, Marine Forces Reservespoke to the Marines that attended the symposium, contributing to discussions focused on strengthening administrative proficiency and ensuring personnel across the Reserve to remain informed of current policies and requirements.

The symposium also provided an opportunity to recognize administrative excellence across the force. Sumruld presented Staff Sgt. Edward Ibarra, a personnel chief with 2nd Battalion, 24th Marines, 4th Marine Division, for the most outstanding multiple site performance on the Marine Corps administrative analysis team inspection award during the symposium. The recognition highlighted the standards of administrative proficiency throughout the symposium and the impact it had on the role of personnel administration in supporting Marines.

Recognition of administrative performance reinforces the symposium’s broader emphasis on maintaining high standards across the personnel and administration occupational field. For administrators, supporting the Reserve component and maintaining proficiency is important because the field is highly technical and subject to frequent policy and regulatory updates.

By strengthening administrative proficiency, recognizing excellence and connecting administrators with resources across the force, the FY26 Senior Personnel Administration Training Symposium supports Marine Forces Reserve ability to maintain an administratively prepared and operationally ready Reserve force.

items.title: Walter Reed marks 15 years while honoring a legacy of military medicine
items.author: Christopher Smith
items.summary: September 2026 marks the 15th anniversary of the establishment of Walter Reed National Military Medical Center, The milestone marks 15 years of unified tri-service care following the historic 2011 consolidation of Walter Reed Army Medical Center and the National Naval Medical Center.
items.body:
This September, Walter Reed National Military Medical Center celebrates its 15th anniversary. Hailed as the nation’s premier military medical facility, the center is renowned for delivering presidential-level care to the nation’s service members, retirees and their beneficiaries.

In 2005, the congressionally mandated Base Realignment and Closure (BRAC) Commission issued Recommendation 169, directing the closure of the historic Walter Reed Army Medical Center (WRAMC) in Washington, D.C., and its integration with the National Naval Medical Center (NNMC) in Bethesda, Maryland, widely known as the President’s Hospital. While the primary focus of BRAC efforts was eliminating administrative redundancies and merging military branch operations, the intensifying conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan transformed what began as a major initiative focused on efficiency into a national mission to modernize combat casualty care.

One of the central intentions of the integration was the unification of the best military medical personnel from all the military branches. Each branch has a clinical presence at WRNMMC, and patients coming to the hospital can be assured of receiving world-class care, no matter what uniform they wear.

Retired U.S. Army Col. (Dr.) Paul Pasquina, chief of WRNMMC’s Department of Rehabilitation, came to Bethesda from “Walter Reed Classic,” as he refers to the former army hospital. He said that while there was some uncertainty about the integration from staff at both locations, the logic in combining the two facilities was clear from the start.

“Walter Reed has international name recognition that people don’t attribute strictly to the Army, Navy or Air Force — they attribute it to the United States of America,” Pasquina said. “And then you had Bethesda Naval Medical Center, which was well known as the President’s Hospital. So, you have the legacy of that reputation, along with its location and its architecture. It just seemed like a win-win.”

The formation of WRNMMC was made that much more complex with the increasing waves of casualties coming from Operations Enduring Freedom and Iraqi Freedom. When compared to the challenges and sacrifices faced by service members and their families, Pasquina said the transition from one facility to the other paled in comparison.

“We were charged with doing something that had never been done before,” Pasquina said. “It comes with an enormous sense of pride that we were able to pull this off, especially when were simultaneously entrusted to provide cutting-edge care to our nation’s heroes – many returning with incredibly complex injuries. It was a responsibility that none of us took lightly.”

To meet the specialized needs created by the influx of those casualties, the medical center required a dramatic physical expansion. The merging of the two facilities on the Bethesda campus offered several advantages. The former Walter Reed hospital covered approximately 1.3 million square feet. The transition to Bethesda increased that figure to an estimated 2.4 million square feet, effectively doubling the medical center’s physical capacity. Additionally, the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences already shared grounds with NNMC, where many Walter Reed clinicians served as faculty and attended as students.

Carolyn Stoneburner is the administrator to the director for dentistry at WRNMMC, and she transitioned to Bethesda during the BRAC process.

“As we celebrate the 15th anniversary of Walter Reed National Military Medical Center, I’m reminded of where this journey began for so many of us — at the former Walter Reed Army Medical Center,” Stoneburner said.“I was fortunate to be part of the Walter Reed family during the BRAC transition, which was a time of tremendous change, uncertainty and new beginnings.While the buildings and the name may have changed, the heart of Walter Reed never did. The dedication, compassion, professionalism, and commitment to those who serve have continued from the old Walter Reed to the WRNMMC we know today.”

For Stoneburner, the consolidation only reinforced the dedication staff brought to their patients across both campuses.

“Fifteen years later, I look back with pride and gratitude for the people I served alongside, the patients we cared for, and the legacy we carried forward. The place changed, the mission continued, and the legacy lives on. Happy 15th anniversary to Walter Reed National Military Medical Center — and to everyone who has been part of the Walter Reed story,” Stoneburner said.

In addition to the establishment of WRNMMC, there are two other significant dates in September that highlight important milestones along the history of WRNMMC.

“Not only is September 2026 the 15th anniversary of WRNMMC, it’s also the 175th anniversary of the birth of U.S. Army Major (Dr.) Walter Reed, the medical center's namesake,” said retired U.S. Army Col. (Dr.) John Pierce, president of the Walter Reed Society. “It’s also the 125th anniversary of his world-changing research in Cuba demonstrating yellow fever was transmitted by the bite of a common domestic mosquito.”

That more than century-old commitment to clinical discovery and innovation remains at the heart of WRNMMC and its mission today. For Pasquina, that shared heritage goes beyond branch rivalries to serve a higher national calling.

“It's Walter Reed National Military Medical Center. Nowhere in that title does it say Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force, Marines, or Coast Guard,” Pasquina said. “It is the nation's medical center, and as many senior leaders have said, it is recognized for excellence across the globe. And in order to maintain that excellence, we need the best and brightest that the military has to offer, no matter what color uniform they wear.”

To learn more about the history of WRNMMC and the two prior facilities, visit walterreed.tricare.mil/About-Us/Facilities/Our-Rich-History .

items.title: Air Force Eyes New-Build F-16s to Boost Fighter Force
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: The Air Force will consider acquiring new F-16 Fighting Falcon jets to answer capacity shortfalls in its aging fighter fleet, according to multiple people familiar with the matter. These discussions are happening as the Air Force is building its proposed fiscal 2028 budget and the five-year spending plan that goes with it. The post Air Force Eyes New-Build F-16s to Boost Fighter Force appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .<
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

The Air Force will consider acquiring new F-16 Fighting Falcon jets to help fill capacity shortfalls in its aging fighter fleet, multiple people familiar with the matter told Air & Space Forces Magazine. These discussions are happening as the Air Force is building its proposed fiscal 2028 budget and the five-year spending plan that goes with it.

Buying new F-16s—which would be the U.S.’s first in more than 20 years—is viewed as one way to quickly build back lost fighter capacity, as Lockheed Martin continues to operate a hot production line for the aircraft. Buying F-16s from Lockheed, which also produces the F-35 Lightning II, would have parallels to the decision to acquire F-15EX Eagle IIs from Boeing, which likewise came after a yearslong gap in USAF purchases.

The new-build F-16s, potentially dubbed “F-16G” to reflect upgrades from existing F-16C and D models, could be on the agenda for discussion when Air Force four-stars gather this fall for a Corona gathering of top service officials.

Lockheed Martin deferred questions to the Air Force: “This topic is best addressed by the U.S. government, but we stand ready to support the U.S. Air Force and its mission needs,” Lockheed said in a statement. “Our proven products are the backbone of the USAF fleet and provide the most advanced and versatile capabilities to ensure air dominance now and decades to come.”

The Air Force, in a written response to Air & Space Forces Magazine, said it is examining its options as it looks to the future.

“The Department of the Air Force is in initial phases of analyzing options for the next Future Years Defense Program,” an Air Force spokesperson said. “At this stage, we have neither defined the precise mission requirements nor the spectrum of options that could fill it.”

Lockheed currently produces F-16E and F models, single- and dual-seat variants respectively, for the United Arab Emirates. The company moved its production line for Block 70 F-16s in 2019 from Fort Worth, Texas, to Greenville, S.C.

If the Air Force decided to buy more F-16s, Lockheed would likely keep its Greenville production line going. The potential upgraded F-16 from that line is being referred to as a G model by those familiar with the discussions.

The Air Force today has 826 F-16s in its inventory, with 484 of those operated by the Active-Duty force. The jets average 34 years old, however, and the newest in the inventory have been flying since 2005.

USAF F-16s carry out a variety of critical missions, including air-to-air and air-to-ground strikes. F-16s that carry out suppression of enemy air defense missions are referred to as “Wild Weasels” and have seen heavy action in operations against Iran.

New F-16 purchases would drive other movement in the industry. Both Pratt & Whitney and GE Aerospace make engines that go on the F-16. Pratt, which is owned by RTX, announced Sept. 15 it has licensed Hermeus to manufacture its F100-PW-229 used on the F-15 and F-16, saying the agreement will strengthen the U.S. defense industrial base by creating a new source for the widely used engine.

Northrop Grumman, which is developing two major upgrades for existing F-16s, would also likely benefit. The company is working on the Integrated Viper Electronic Warfare Suite, or IVEWS, and an upgraded large aperture targeting pod called LITENING LA.

IVEWS, also known as the AN/ALQ-257, is an advanced electronic warfare system providing radar warning, active jamming, and detecting, identifying and locating of potential threats.

A source familiar with the issue, who asked not to be named to speak more freely, said any new F-16 would likely have IVEWS and multiple other new capabilities placing it not only beyond the legacy C and D fighters, but also the Block 70 fighters Lockheed is currently building.

“If the Air Force were to buy a new F-16, this would not be your grandfather’s F-16,” the source said. “This would be more akin to buying an F-15EX.”

The source said buying more F-16s would make sense for the Air Force, since Lockheed and Boeing are facing capacity constraints limiting how many F-35As and F-15EXs, respectively, they can build. And the service’s existing fleet of F-16s has been flown hard in the wars of recent decades, the source said.

“There’s only so many times you can do a service life extension program before you begin to lose the strength and integrity of the airframe itself,” the source said.
